Supply-demand imbalance update: no change on EMLs (still shipping behind customer demand, previously cited at greater than 30%), but high-powered lasers have deteriorated sharply - 'we are way behind in our shipments... The demand signal has increased, and we are very much further behind relative to our ability to supply.' Management clarified the ramp execution itself is on track; the gap widened because demand accelerated. High-powered lasers were named as the one vector that materially changed since the prior quarter.
EML imbalance unchanged (>30%); high-power laser shortfall materially worse on accelerating demand

Pump lasers: shipments surged more than 80% year-over-year and Lumentum will 'remain effectively sold out for the foreseeable future despite our rapid capacity expansion.' A fourfold increase in pump laser shipments is still expected over the next several quarters. Share is roughly 70%-80%. Capacity is ramping at Rose Orchard (US) with packaging and test in Thailand. Multiple long-term customer agreements have been secured to help offset planned capital expenditures - mostly three-year arrangements with built-in pricing levers and, in most instances, take-or-pay structures, formed largely with NEMs (network equipment manufacturers).
pump lasers +80% YoY; 4x shipment increase expected; ~70-80% share; 3-year take-or-pay LTAs

InP substrate supply: after a surge in ultra-high-power laser demand across a couple of customers, Lumentum spent the last three months securing additional substrate supply and signed a deal with AXT during the quarter. Hurlston: 'we went out and we found additional substrate help from AXT. They are a great partner.' Lumentum is comfortable near-term on the strength of its lead arrangement with a Japanese supplier plus the AXT deal, but flagged that given the rate of change in the demand vector 'that may not be true a quarter or two from now either' - more substrate help is likely needed if the vector continues.
AXT InP substrate deal signed in Q4; more substrate supply likely needed if demand vector continues

Balance sheet / working capital: completed $5.6B of equity offerings in Q4 ($1.4B common stock + $4.2B mandatory convertible preferred), cash $7.5B, borrowings + converts $8.7B, net debt cut to $1.2B from $7.5B; no plan to use the ATM program. Q4 operating cash flow +$747M and free cash flow $722M on $28M capex (FY2026 operating cash flow -$6.8B, capex $162M). Closing inventory $12.9B, up from $11.1B, built ahead of higher FY2027 revenue; cash conversion cycle 149 days (from 106) - DIO 119, DSO 59, DPO 29 - expected to normalize on the tighter contract terms written into the current backlog. Inventory/generation-transition risk managed with non-cancellable POs, procurement matched to shipment schedules, and building-block subsystems reusable across product lines and generations.
$5.6B raise; net debt $1.2B; inventory $12.9B; CCC 149 days

Component procurement scaled ahead of the FY2027 ramp: closing inventory $12.9B, up from $11.1B, built in anticipation of higher revenue; the $5.6B June equity raise is described as fully supporting component supply and business needs. Generation-transition risk on memory and other components is managed with non-cancellable POs, procurement matched to shipment schedules, and building-block subsystems that stay compatible across product lines and generations - with management noting that with prices rising so fast, older inventory has often been resold favorably.

Record demand and de-concentrating customer base: over $60B of NEW ORDERS booked in Q4 FY2026 (~70% pure AI, ~30% CPU / CPU-based AI / edge AI), taking order book and backlog to record levels entering FY2027. NINE customers exceeded $1B of revenue in FY2026 versus four in FY2025, and the largest datacenter/CSP customer was 28% of FY2026 revenue. The $1B+ cohort is described as a lot of emerging Neoclouds and CSPs plus some enterprise customers. FY2027 revenue guided to $65-72B.
$60B+ new orders in Q4 (70% pure AI); 9 customers >$1B vs 4; top customer 28%

Deployment timing, not demand, is the constraint: Q4 revenue of $11.1B landed near the low end of guidance because large datacenter and Neocloud customers were not ready on power, cooling and networking - a timing story with the revenue expected in subsequent quarters, and OEM/large-DC revenue fell 26% QoQ to $5.5B while enterprise/channel doubled. September and December quarter order/shipment activity described as quite strong. On the ODM-disintermediation concern, management positions Supermicro as running BOTH an OEM and an ODM model and says it will keep growing in both. DCBBS is pitched as the answer to the readiness problem - a one-stop shop (power, DLC, CDU, chill door, water tower, 1.6T switching, management software, lifecycle service) that lets customers build AI datacenters in quarters rather than years and improves time-to-deployment (TTD) and time-to-online (TTO).
Q4 $11.1B (low end) on customer power/cooling/network readiness; OEM+ODM both

MEMORY SHORTAGE SPILLOVER INTO OPTICS: 100G revenue will DECLINE in Q3 because one customer cannot source enough 100G SWITCHES to meet its forecast - management attributes the switch shortage to the MEMORY SHORTAGE and expects 100G weakness to persist 'until the memory supply recovers' (CEO: back to normal 'within a few months, either by end of this year or next year'). Quantified impact: ~$20-25M of lost 100G single-mode transceiver revenue in Q3; without it Q3 growth would be >50% Q/Q instead of ~35-45%.
-$20M to -$25M of Q3 100G revenue lost to the memory-driven switch shortage

CPO / ELSFP EXTERNAL LASER SOURCE ECONOMICS: ELSFP (external light source for co-packaged optics) is in very limited production now, ramping later in 2026 and through 2027 to ~400,000 PIECES PER MONTH IN 2028. Laser power scaling is the constraint: CPO/ELSFP uses a 300mW laser vs 70mW in an 800G transceiver and 100mW in a 1.6T transceiver, with die size ~6x larger, so meeting CPO demand requires the industry laser market to be 8-10x BIGGER than today; the next generation of ELSFP moves to DWDM, where yield loss is 40-50% worse than 1310nm. Laser capacity carries a 21-24 MONTH equipment-to-high-volume lead time. AOI is engaged with ~5 CPO customers on 3-4 year demand; several have already qualified AOI on fixed-wavelength CPO laser / ELSFP, with DWDM the current focus. High-volume ELSFP manufacturing is 'more like late Q3 next year' (late 2027). Houston laser fab capacity to grow ~300% by Q3 2027 plus a SECOND FAB cleanroom ~4x the size of the current facility (adding MOCVD, epi, steppers). Margin mix: laser gross margin 55-65%, ELSFP module ('EOSAP') >50%, both landing H2 2027. AOI is absent from first-generation CPO deployments purely because laser capacity must first feed AOI's own transceivers.
ELSFP ~400k pcs/month in 2028; 300mW CPO laser vs 70mW(800G)/100mW(1.6T); industry laser capacity needs 8-10x; laser GM 55-65%

BOTTLENECK HAS MOVED FROM LASERS TO DSP/TIA: because AOI makes its own lasers in-house it avoids the laser shortage that management calls 'the biggest bottleneck right now for the transceiver business' and 'the number one issue' for competitors; AOI's binding constraints for 800G/1.6T are instead DSP and TIA supply, where 'the whole supply chain is very tight' for 1.6T - AOI says its supplier ranks it FOURTH priority under a long-term partnership, with calls once or twice a week. INDIUM PHOSPHIDE SUBSTRATE: supply secured into end-2027 and 'incrementally better' than last quarter - not currently a limiter; AOI has just moved to 4-INCH substrate volume manufacturing and buys from 2 European + 2 Japanese + 3 Chinese suppliers, and is negotiating partnerships or a possible JOINT VENTURE with 2-3 of them for 2028-2029 volumes (laser capacity growing 'much more than a factor of 10'). Proprietary in-house production machinery insulates AOI from the industry's equipment-delivery bottlenecks.
DSP/TIA = binding constraint (AOI ranked 4th priority); InP substrate secured to end-2027; 4-inch substrate volume production

Named by AOI management on its Q2 FY2026 call as one of the very few suppliers able to serve the high-power CPO laser market: AOI, Lumentum, Coherent and Broadcom are all 'invest[ing] huge money' in laser capacity, yet 'even combined... it's still very tough to meet the customer demand in the next few years'. Sizing: CPO/ELSFP needs a 300mW laser (vs 70mW for 800G, 100mW for 1.6T) with ~6x larger die, so the industry laser market must grow 8-10x; DWDM ELSFP carries 40-50% worse yield loss than 1310nm, and laser equipment takes 21-24 months from order to high-volume output. AOI states only AOI, Lumentum and Coherent can hit acceptable DWDM CPO laser / CPO module yields.
Industry high-power laser capacity must grow 8-10x for CPO; 21-24 month equipment lead time

SUPPLY-CHAIN RAMP is the bottleneck, not demand. Two new contract-manufacturing sites missed: (1) Houston, USA — a fully automated enclosure plant with 15 GWh/year capacity that Fluence off-takes, run by the SAME contract manufacturer that operates its main Vietnam enclosure facility. Delayed a few months by construction, automation-equipment issues and a utility-interconnection delay (the plant has been running on generators, preventing parallel commissioning work); limited production started in Q3, grid connection expected within weeks, FULL production in fiscal Q1 2027. (2) One of two new facilities in China — initial production of Smartstack components (the 'pods' that sit on the skids) failed Fluence's testing and required rework; corrections are implemented, shipping has resumed and the site reached full production in Q4. Management put a hedge and a contingency in the plan and blew through both. Organizational response: Roman Loosen (Chief Enterprise Operations Officer, 20+ years at Siemens) takes over supply chain and manufacturing and Peter Williams moves to product, both reporting to the CEO; framed as an EXECUTION/process-scaling fix, not a change of suppliers. Once Houston is fully ramped, Fluence expects domestic-content capacity sufficient for its entire current backlog.
Houston 15 GWh/yr, full production fiscal Q1 2027; China site reworked, full production in Q4; ~$400M of FY26 revenue pushed to FY27

SOURCING: Fluence signed a long-term battery-cell agreement with an INTERNATIONAL supplier that covers not just supply but technology-roadmap alignment on how cells behave inside Fluence's modules — securing long-term volume and attractive pricing for FY2027-28 and letting it price future orders with more confidence, at the cost of a $15M charge on one in-flight project supplied by the same counterparty. Explicitly NOT related to AESC (the AESC review, run earlier in the year, drove some strategic expense but produced no announcement); Fluence says it is spending a lot of time talking to battery capacity across the market and sees an opportunity to work more closely with U.S. battery manufacturers. On inverters: Fluence uses ONLY non-Chinese inverters in the U.S. — mostly U.S.-made, some imported from Europe — so it expects zero impact from the FCC's inverter restrictions; in Europe it still uses a mix of Chinese and non-Chinese and is working toward a fully European solution ahead of expected European restrictions.
Long-term cell supply + tech-roadmap agreement (int'l supplier, not AESC), $15M charge; 100% non-Chinese inverters in the U.S.

Capacity and balance sheet: NOT capacity constrained - in-house factories support ~$2B of revenue and the Asian EXTENDED FACTORIES have now added essentially an equal amount of capability, with shorter cycle times, second shifts running and third shifts available; the extended-factory model also cut freight and labor cost and lowered capex needs, a large driver of the 2026 margin expansion. Supply chain is called the residual risk, managed by 'leveraging our balance sheet' to build inventory. Nearly $1.9B of cash and short-term investments; $62M operating cash flow (>100% of net income); May completion of a $1.5B 0%-coupon convertible due 2031 (~$1.2B net cash) plus ~$200M of buyback and a capped call struck at $509.06. Analyst day set for December 17 at the NYSE
capacity ~$2B in-house + equal from extended factories; cash ~$1.9B

NEW-BUILD ECONOMICS GAP: ERCOT year-to-date wholesale power has averaged $30/MWh (same as last year) versus the ~$90/MWh area cited for new-build contracting — '30 is not going to get new stuff built.' The price of generation EQUIPMENT 'has doubled, if not tripled' in some cases, so what was an acceptable build price a year or two ago no longer is. In PJM the $555/MW-day RPB cap 'might get some things built' but a spread around it will be needed for certain projects. Large-load customers are willing to contract with EXISTING assets at a PREMIUM because it is still a discount to new build; co-location can beat even an islanded new build on speed.
ERCOT YTD $30/MWh vs ~$90 new build; equipment costs 2-3x; PJM RPB cap $555/MW-day

Market outlook: the NAND market is estimated to EXCEED $300 BILLION in calendar 2026 (up 3x YoY) and to APPROACH $500 BILLION in calendar 2027. Data center's share of total NAND TAM expands from ~30% in CY2025 to ~50% in CY2026 and continues outpacing the market in 2027. Demand from customers is growing faster than Sandisk's supply, so bits are expected to REMAIN ON ALLOCATION BEYOND CALENDAR 2027. Sandisk plans to grow with the market rather than outgrow it, holding segment share.
NAND TAM >$300B CY2026 (3x YoY) -> ~$500B CY2027; DC share 30% -> ~50%; on allocation past CY2027

VISIBILITY EXTENDING TO 2031: having previously disclosed one large-customer LTA running to CY2029, WD is now 'in the throes of discussions' to establish LTAs for CALENDAR 2029, 2030 AND 2031 - volume line of sight is described as good, with the open item being the pricing/commercial construct. Forward exabyte demand growth guided at 25%+ (Q4's +22% framed as mix lumpiness - customers taking more CMR in a given quarter ship fewer bits per unit than UltraSMR-heavy customers - not a demand signal). THE BUYER BASE IS BROADENING BEYOND HYPERSCALERS: neoclouds, FRONTIER AI LABS and sovereigns are now coming directly for supply, and one AUTONOMOUS-VEHICLE customer's CY2027 exabyte demand has increased MULTIPLE-FOLD. Enterprise OEMs are also pivoting BACK TOWARD HYBRID storage after flirting with 100% all-flash arrays, adding further demand. In a 'very tight supply environment' these newer buyers give WD increased pricing leverage
LTA talks now cover CY2029/2030/2031; 25%+ forward exabyte growth; AV customer CY2027 demand up multiple-fold

CALL — HELIOS RAMP AND ECONOMICS: Helios is IN PRODUCTION with initial shipments beginning later in Q3, a step-up in Q4, a FURTHER step-up in Q1 2027, and a ramp through 2027; customer pull is 'very strong and TRACKING AHEAD OF OUR INITIAL FORECASTS' (a volume statement, per Lisa Su). Across inferencing workloads Helios delivers UP TO 15% MORE THROUGHPUT AT THE SAME RACK POWER and UP TO 30% MORE TOKENS PER DOLLAR than the competition, and carries ~50% more HBM than competing racks. Yields on the highly complex product are expected to improve over the next few quarters. Beyond the gigawatt-scale anchors (OpenAI, Meta, Anthropic — consuming via multiple CSPs), 'lots of customers' are interested at more regular scale, with good customer diversity expected by Q4/Q1. New Cerebras partnership: Helios plus Cerebras' Wafer Scale Engine forms a disaggregated FAST-INFERENCE solution available in Q4 in the Cerebras Cloud, extending into 2027. Supply: 'we have supply to more than meet the guidance... and the upside potential is there'; no data-center readiness constraint (land/power/shell) that threatens targets, though the range depends on how fast operators bring capacity online.
Helios: production now, ships late Q3 -> Q4 step-up -> Q1'27 step-up; +15% throughput/same power, +30% tokens/$; pull ahead of forecast

FIFTH consecutive quarter of record server CPU revenue: cloud AND enterprise each grew MORE THAN 70% YoY (beating the prior-quarter outlook), with double-digit growth in BOTH units and ASPs (units higher; ASPs up on core-count mix). x86 server revenue share gained YoY on Turin + Genoa. Turin now powers nearly ONE-THIRD of the >1,600 EPYC public-cloud instance types; >230 fifth-gen EPYC platforms in market; enterprise logged a FOURTH straight record sell-through quarter. Outlook stepped up sharply: server revenue +>80% YoY in H2 2026 and +>70% for FULL-YEAR 2027 off a much higher base; server CPU TAM raised to >50% annual growth reaching ~$220 BILLION by 2030 (vs >$120B guided just one quarter ago) — with AGENTIC-AI SANDBOX SERVERS the largest and fastest-growing bucket of that 2030 TAM (vs general-purpose and AI head-nodes). Server CPU supply is TIGHT ('much of this demand was unforecasted'); AMD is raising wafer, back-end and substrate capacity through 2026 and expects 2027 supply to be better than 2026.
5th record qtr; cloud & enterprise each +>70%; H2-26 server +>80%; FY27 +>70%; TAM ~$220B by 2030; supply tight

VENICE (Zen 6, 2nm) IS IN PRODUCTION NOW — one of the largest generational gains in EPYC history: MORE THAN 2x the performance per watt of leading x86 CPUs and up to 3.3x the performance per watt of leading Arm-based CPUs, across a family of MORE THAN 30 PROCESSORS. Every major OEM is on track to launch platforms and leading cloud providers plan deployments beginning later this year; customer demand for Venice is STRONGER THAN FOR ANY PRIOR EPYC GENERATION, and the workload set expands vs Turin. On 2nm capacity: AMD's chiplet approach means it ramps FEWER WAFERS on the new node than monolithic competitors, easing the leading-edge supply constraint.
Venice in production: >2x perf/W vs x86, 3.3x vs Arm, 30+ SKUs; chiplets = fewer 2nm wafers needed

CALL — SUPPLY IS TIGHTENING AND AI-DC GETS PRIORITY: 'Supply is tightening in several growth areas, LEAD TIMES ARE EXTENDING' — average lead times stretched from ~27 TO ~32 WEEKS — with rising ORDERS PLACED WITHIN LEAD TIME and CUSTOMER ESCALATIONS; book-to-bill 'significantly above one for several quarters and continued to strengthen'; visibility improving into 2027 with SOME CUSTOMERS ORDERING INTO 2028 to lock supply. In Q2 onsemi PRIORITIZED AI-DATA-CENTER SHIPMENTS OVER AUTOMOTIVE AND INDUSTRIAL (normalizing in Q3/Q4 as output catches up; fab cycle 4-6 months). Utilization jumped 77% -> 83% (~92-93% = fully utilized; revenue could run 25-30% above current rate before capping; ~2-quarter lag to P&L -> Q3 GM guided to a STEP-UP 40-42%, sequential expansion all year at ~25-30bps per utilization point). Pricing: input costs rising (substrates, gold, external manufacturing) -> SECOND ROUND of price increases, plus surgical increases where allocation exists; 'NOTHING IS COMING DOWN... I'm not expecting a softer pricing environment in 2027 either.' Portfolio reshaping DONE: final $35M of non-core exits (~$300M in 2026, ~$900M cumulative); Mountain Top + Philippines fabs divested (~$35M savings from 2027, ~50 of 200bps planned FabRight GM gain); NO customer inventory build — shipping to end demand, channel at 10.1 weeks with sell-through > sell-in; mass market +20% QoQ.
Lead times 27 -> 32 wks; orders into 2027/2028; AI-DC prioritized over auto/industrial; 2nd price round; Q3 GM step-up to 40-42%

Record ATM (OSAT) revenue NTD 126.1B (+12% QoQ, +36% YoY) with ATM gross margin 27.3% and operating margin 15.7%; full-year 2026 ATM revenue expected to grow ~35%. Capacity is the binding constraint — blended utilization 80-85% but 'generally very close to being full', with near-term growth gated by equipment installation and building construction. Q4 2026 ATM gross margin is likely to EXCEED the 30% structural ceiling, after which management will review raising the 26-29% structural margin range upward; pricing environment described as friendly, with material and component cost inflation passed through to customers.
ATM record NTD 126.1B (+36% YoY), GM 27.3%; Q4 GM to break the 30% structural ceiling

LEAP (leading-edge advanced packaging) revenue is tracking ~USD 200M AHEAD of the USD 3.5B 2026 guidance and management is aiming to DOUBLE LEAP revenue in 2027. Full-process CoWoS-like packaging is on track for ~USD 300M in 2026 with substantial growth in 2027 and is expected to be margin-accretive. ASE's fully automated PANEL line (310mm x 310mm) enters production in Q1 2027, complementary to foundry CoWoS and serving the same customer set at similar reticle size and pitch. Capacity — not demand — is the constraint: blended utilization 80-85% but effectively full, with growth gated by equipment installation and building construction (13 greenfield plus 8 brownfield projects underway). FY2026 capex raised USD 2B to ~USD 10.5B, ~70% of equipment capex going to leading edge.
LEAP ~USD 3.7B 2026, DOUBLING in 2027; full-process ~USD 300M; panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027

CAPACITY IS THE BINDING CONSTRAINT: blended utilization 80-85%, but 'outside of equipment lines being placed into service, capacities were generally very close to being full' — non-LEAP wire bond and traditional advanced packaging were tight, and wafer sort and final test were running near full. 'Our capability for near-term incremental growth is being gated by our abilities to install capital equipment and build out our buildings and facilities.' Dr. Wu frames HARDWARE INFRASTRUCTURE as the new bottleneck ('we have not experienced this for the last 40 years') and argues packaging is moving up the system-architecture value chain. On the Q3 guide: '12%-13% growth... means we have to add 12%-13% capacity'; all customers are asking for more devices in Q3 and Q4.
utilization 80-85% but effectively full; growth gated by equipment install + building construction

Technology roadmap. PANEL: ASE's fully automated panel line starts PRODUCTION IN Q1 2027 in a 310mm x 310mm form factor — described as COMPLEMENTARY to foundry CoWoS, serving the SAME CUSTOMER SET with identical reticle size and pitch/line-width coverage; adoption depends on capacity, performance and speed of execution. GLASS SUBSTRATE: NOT in production and not within the next 12 months; R&D is evaluating feasibility and economics with substrate suppliers, the foundry and customers. FULL-PROCESS (CoWoS-like): on track for ~USD 300M of revenue in 2026 with aggressive capacity expansion and substantial growth in 2027; margin not yet fully reflected but expected to be margin-accretive. CPO: launching toward the END OF 2026 in initially small volume, yielding benchmark data on bandwidth, system performance and thermal dissipation; more detail promised in two quarters. Bigger reticle sizes drive panel/more-complex CoWoS first, then POWER DELIVERY becomes the next constraint over the following two to three years.
panel 310x310mm production Q1 2027; glass substrate not within 12 months; full-process ~USD 300M 2026; CPO launches late 2026

STRONGEST JUNE QUARTER EVER — leading-edge silicon demand keeps compounding: FQ3 revenue $109.4B, UP 16% year over year, with iPhone, Mac and Services each setting June-quarter records and double-digit growth IN EVERY GEOGRAPHIC SEGMENT. Gross margin 50.1% — including a favorable ~2-percentage-point impact from TARIFF REFUNDS — and diluted EPS $2.02, up 29%. Installed base of active devices at a new all-time high across all major product categories and regions. AI angle: WWDC26 introduced 'the all-new SIRI AI' alongside the latest software platforms — sustaining Apple's pull on TSMC leading-edge capacity (the prior quarter's constraint was explicitly advanced-node availability, not memory).
FQ3 $109.4B (+16%), best June qtr ever; EPS $2.02 (+29%); GM 50.1% incl ~2pts tariff refunds; Siri AI

CALL-ONLY: THE JUNE-QUARTER SHORTFALL WAS A LEADING-EDGE NODE SHORTAGE, AND IT GETS WORSE IN SEPTEMBER. Cook: June-quarter supply constraints hit 'primarily the Mac, and to a lesser extent, iPhone and iPad', and 'the constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the ADVANCED NODES that our SoCs are produced on'. Root cause is 'not a regular supply issue - it's a DEMAND FORECAST issue' (iPhone +22% and Mac +29% ran ahead of Apple's own high expectations). 'We are seeing LESS FLEXIBILITY in the supply chain than normal... we've been pulling supply ahead. At some point, there's a limit to that.' For the September quarter the supply-constraint impact 'increases SIGNIFICANTLY sequentially' and now spans iPhone, Mac AND iPad - 'we've got a quarter that we're going to be scrambling on the supply side'. Asked whether adding a second US fab operator would help, Cook rejected the premise: 'this isn't a partner or supplier issue.'
Sept-qtr constraint impact up SIGNIFICANTLY QoQ; iPhone + Mac + iPad all constrained

CALL-ONLY: MEMORY IS NOW THE ENTIRE MARGIN STORY, QUANTIFIED. CFO Parekh's bridge: total-company GM 49.3% (Mar qtr) -> 48.1% (Jun qtr, ex-tariff-refund) = -120bps, and 'MORE THAN 100% of that can be explained by the MEMORY COST change' - FX 'was a factor' but 'the main driver was really the memory cost impact'. The same holds into the September guide: 48.1% -> 46.5% midpoint (ex-refund) = -160bps, again more than fully explained by memory, with partial offsets from carry-in inventory, lower non-memory component costs and favorable mix. Reported June-quarter GM was 50.1% INCLUDING ~2pts of tariff refunds (products GM 40.1%, +140bps QoQ including >2.5pts of refunds; services GM 75.6%, -110bps on mix). September guide: revenue +9-11% YoY (FX -2.5pts sequential + rising supply constraints), iPhone mid-teens, GM 47-48% incl. ~1pt refunds, opex $19.1-19.4B, tax ~16.5%.
Jun GM 48.1% ex-refund (-120bps, >100% memory-driven); Sep guide GM 47-48%, rev +9-11%

CALL-ONLY: MAC IS BEING BOUGHT AS AI COMPUTE. Mac $10.4B (+29% YoY, June-quarter record) 'despite significant supply constraints', with customers 'using MAC MINI as a powerful platform for AGENTIC AI' and 'deploying CLUSTERS OF MAC STUDIO systems to RUN FRONTIER-CLASS MODELS LOCALLY'; the stated differentiator is 'massive UNIFIED MEMORY BANDWIDTH' plus power-efficient performance and on-device inference. Enterprise pull is explicit - Disney moving creative AI workflows on-device 'to reduce overall CLOUD TOKEN COSTS' and keep IP secure; Credit Agricole on MacBook Pro. On capital intensity for Siri AI, Cook: Apple runs a HYBRID model - 'we use some THIRD-PARTY CLOUD, and we do OUR OWN DATA CENTERS. There will be a mix' - and AI spend is rising both in OpEx (opex $19.1B, +23% YoY on R&D) and 'other locations on the P&L other than OpEx, like COGS'. Siri AI (WWDC26) is in developer + public beta; EU launch still unresolved with the Commission (Mac exempt from those rules), China approved only for the original Apple Intelligence features so far.
Mac $10.4B (+29%); Mac Studio clusters run frontier models locally; hybrid own-DC + 3rd-party cloud

→ TSMC: Leading-edge node availability at TSMC is Apple's binding constraint, and it TIGHTENS into the September quarter: 'the constraints were primarily driven by the availability of the advanced nodes that our SoCs are produced on', with the impact set to 'increase significantly sequentially' across iPhone, Mac AND iPad and 'less flexibility in the supply chain than normal' after Apple already pulled supply ahead. TSMC's Arizona fab has ramped in Apple's favour - 'we do source over 100 million components this year out of Arizona... we could not be more pleased with how that fab has ramped and is producing for us' - but Cook stressed the shortfall 'isn't a partner or supplier issue'; it is Apple's own demand forecast running behind an iPhone +22% / Mac +29% cycle.
units: >100M components sourced from TSMC Arizona in 2026

Supply chain is the binding constraint on the AGI CPU ramp, not demand: 'It is a very tight market across everything. Whether it's memory, whether it's test equipment, whether it's substrates, whether it's TSMC wafers' — Rene Haas noting even CPU rivals with their own fabs 'have not been able to supply the demand'. Confidence improved across ALL of wafers, substrates, test capacity and memory over the past 90 days, and management sees no single-point-of-failure component risk. Relief is expected as capacity expands into calendar 2028-2029 (FY2029-FY2030), where wafer and memory capacity estimates are up ~70-100%.
wafers/substrates/test/memory all tight; capacity +70-100% by CY2028-29

TAM reframing: Arm's March view of a $100B+ data-center CPU market (up from a $50-60B consensus at the time) now looks conservative — peers have since cited numbers up to $200B+, with the most recent estimate around $220B. Arm is NOT changing its published numbers (the $15B AGI CPU / FY2031 framework stands) but flagged the same market share against a $200B+ TAM would imply material upside; internal targets are higher than external. Driver: inference-based compute running agentic workloads is throughput-constrained by CPU count, so rising inference and agentic demand converts directly into CPU demand.
DC CPU TAM $100B (Mar) -> ~$220B external estimates; Arm numbers unchanged

CALL-ONLY / THE DDR SNAP-BACK, SEEN FROM THE PROBE-CARD SIDE: Q3 DRAM revenue is guided COMPARABLE to the record Q2 'but with a significant underlying SHIFT FROM HBM TO DDR'. The reason is the memory shortage itself - 'as you've heard recently from all our major DRAM customers, the supply environment continues to be EXTREMELY CONSTRAINED, and our customers are shifting their WAFER START MIX TO DDR DESIGNS to capture the profit opportunity provided by significant DDR PRICE INCREASES'. Because probe cards are specific to each customer chip design, FormFactor's mix tracks those wafer-start shifts one-for-one - making its DRAM mix a near-real-time proxy for where DRAM makers are actually pointing capacity 'while these unusual end market conditions persist'.

AI test intensity is compounding because design margins are shrinking: higher data rates, lower latency and the requirement that AI fabrics be LOSSLESS mean customers 'can no longer guarantee anything by design' and must test in production too. A compute or switch tray has gone from tens to HUNDREDS of IC pinouts - more insertion points - tested at signal level (VNAs, oscilloscopes), at bit level (new portfolio) and at protocol/packet level (AI workload emulators). The move from monolithic chips to CHIPLET architectures adds interoperability emulation, and customers now ask for emulation environments that stress a chip while it exercises a model (thermal shutdown, all cores active at higher power and speed). The ecosystem is shifting from a homogeneous integrated vertical stack to a HETEROGENEOUS one - GPU/CPU/DPU mixes and a growing number of protocols at every layer of the stack - which broadens Keysight's addressable tail. The four wireline pillars (AI infrastructure scaling, speed transitions, silicon photonics, system-level emulation) all drove growth. Hyperscaler engagement (rooted in the Ixia acquisition ~5 years ago) is deepening as they integrate Keysight pre-silicon emulation and workload solutions into their development pipelines; hyperscalers plus the model companies are ~10% OF REVENUE DIRECTLY but drive large downstream influence, and many are building their own in-house silicon. Switch designers use Keysight emulators to validate network performance across AI workloads and protocols; interconnect manufacturers use high-fidelity analyzers to characterize high-speed backplanes for signal integrity and manufacturing yield.

Indium phosphide is the binding constraint across the portfolio (assembly and test capacity is available); June-quarter InP laser output — the lasers that feed both 800G and 1.6T transceivers — was up about 80% YoY, and internal InP capacity doubles YoY by the end of the September quarter, one quarter ahead of plan.
800G still growing YoY through CY2026; InP laser output +80% YoY; InP is the constraint

Both transceiver tiers grow together: 800G revenue continues rising year-over-year through calendar 2026 while 1.6T ramps rapidly into 2027 as adoption broadens. Q4 data center revenue +24% QoQ, +66% YoY, the third consecutive quarter of double-digit sequential growth. Supply, not demand, is the limiter — indium phosphide capacity is the primary constraint (assembly and test have headroom), with internal InP output doubling YoY by the end of the September quarter and more than doubling again by end of calendar 2027.
800G + 1.6T both growing; DC revenue +66% YoY; InP the primary constraint

OCS addressable market held at MORE THAN $4 BILLION (doubled from $2B at OFC 2026, 2030 timeframe) and management suggests even that may be conservative — applications have widened from the original scale-out focus to scale-across and now a clear path to SCALE-UP, where there are active customer engagements. OCS revenue grew sequentially in Q4 and is expected to grow significantly through fiscal 2027 as production expands across two manufacturing locations, spanning the 320x320 platform and other system sizes. 1.6T transceivers are ramping rapidly through calendar 2026 into 2027, with the ramp pulled in versus the prior quarter's assumptions.
OCS TAM >$4B and widening to scale-up; OCS revenue growing across two plants; 1.6T ramp pulled in

Segment detail. DATA CENTER AND COMMUNICATIONS segment +40% for FY2026; Q4 +19% QoQ and +59% YoY. DATA CENTER business +41% FY2026; Q4 +24% QoQ and +66% YoY — a third consecutive quarter of double-digit sequential growth, with strong sequential growth expected again in Q1. COMMUNICATIONS +54% FY2026; Q4 +11% QoQ and +56% YoY on data-center interconnect, scale-across and traditional telecom, with particular strength in ZR/ZR+ DCI transceivers, pump lasers and complex high-end optical subsystems. INDUSTRIAL was roughly flat pro forma in both FY2026 and Q4 — semiconductor and display capital equipment grew but were offset by broader industrial weakness; growth is expected to resume led by semicap, where bookings continue to strengthen. Within transceivers, 800G revenue keeps growing YoY through calendar 2026 while 1.6T ramps rapidly through the balance of 2026 into 2027, with the 1.6T ramp PULLED IN and stronger than management assumed three months ago.
Q4 data center +66% YoY, comms +56% YoY; 1.6T ramp pulled in vs 3 months ago

EMLs delivered another record-breaking quarter, primarily driven by 100G-per-lane devices. 200G EMLs are accelerating and now account for over 25% of total EML revenue; management expects 200G EMLs to be 50% or more of volume by mid-calendar-2027. Lumentum remains on track to deliver over 50% EML unit growth in the December 2026 quarter versus the year-ago quarter, but expects to remain significantly behind demand even at year end.
record EML quarter; 200G EML >25% of EML revenue; >50% EML unit growth by Dec-2026 quarter

Cloud transceivers: record 800G shipments in the quarter while initiating production of next-generation 1.6T modules. Transceiver profitability continues to improve on yield gains, capacity utilization, and the initial rollout of higher-ASP 1.6T units. 1.6T uptake is expected to intensify starting in fiscal Q1 FY2027 and sustain through calendar 2027, anchored by lead Tier 1 hyperscale customers rolling out custom AI clusters. Management believes Lumentum is first to market ahead of larger competitors in many instances and can hold that share advantage through the cycle, crediting its signal integrity team on difficult 1.6T designs.
record 800G shipments; 1.6T production initiated; 1.6T uptake intensifies from fiscal Q1 FY2027

Helios and MI450 ship into the same DCBBS total-solution motion - liquid-cooled rack, CDU, networking, management software and lifecycle service - with capacity heading to >6,000 racks/month including >3,000 DLC racks/month at up to 250kW per rack.
Helios product line + Instinct MI450 total solution LAUNCHED

Long-term NVIDIA partnership: shipping VOLUME SKUs across the GB200 NVL72, HGX B200, NVIDIA B200 NVL4 and NVIDIA RTX 6000 Pro product lines. AI solutions were ~60% of Q4 revenue (vs >80% in Q3) on the timing of some large AI project ramps; based on backlog, >80% of revenue is expected to be AI-related going forward, and ~70% of the $60B+ of new Q4 orders is pure AI.
shipping GB200 NVL72 / HGX B200 / B200 NVL4 / RTX 6000 Pro in volume

Preparing to be FIRST TO MARKET on the Rubin generation - Rubin, Vera Rubin NVL72, Rubin HGX, Vera CPU and other high-density Vera systems - alongside the shipping Blackwell lines. Rubin and Vera platforms are liquid-cooling-ready (Vera is CPU-based and much of Supermicro's Vera volume will also be liquid cooled); DLC capacity is being built to >3,000 DLC racks/month, most lines supporting 250kW-class rack platforms. first-to-market target for Rubin / Vera Rubin NVL72 / Rubin HGX / Vera CPU

1.6T RAMP BEGINS: full qualification of AOI's first 1.6T product at the hyperscale customer expected 'within the next couple of weeks', with 1.6T shipments starting later in Q3 - AOI says it will be the FOURTH supplier qualified at that one big hyperscale data center customer for 1.6T. The customer returns to 10%+ of revenue in Q3. The previously announced order is now sized at MORE THAN $200M in hand: deliveries start very late Q3, the BULK ships in Q4, with a tail into Q1 2027 (target to complete by ~Q2 2027) - and management frames it as 'just the very beginning' of significant recurring 1.6T orders. Q4 1.6T revenue commitment $70-80M (limited by MATERIAL supply, not capacity); Q1 2027 1.6T revenue targeted to DOUBLE Q4 or more. Q4 combined 800G+1.6T revenue of ~$330M confirmed 'about right, directionally'. Longer term, customer feedback points to >500,000 1.6T transceivers/month by end-2027 = $300-350M/month.
>$200M 1.6T orders in hand; Q4 1.6T $70-80M; Q4 800G+1.6T ~$330M; >500k units/mo ($300-350M/mo) by end-2027

CAPACITY RAMP: 800G/1.6T manufacturing capacity is 'approaching 200,000 units per month' now, up from ~100,000/month exiting Q1 FY2026; expected to reach OVER 650,000 pieces/month by END-2026 and OVER 930,000 pieces/month by END-2027, with MORE THAN HALF of that output from TEXAS. Texas footprint expanded to OVER 1.6 MILLION sq ft in greater Houston (vs ~900k sq ft reported at Q1 FY2026 and only ~65,000 sq ft a year ago). The 210k sq ft facility (dedicated 800G/1.6T) starts initial production LATE in Q3; moving transceiver lines out of headquarters frees that fab to expand INDIUM PHOSPHIDE wafer capacity; Pearland (construction started) and Houston buildouts come online EARLY 2027. Capacity is 'complete book already from now until Q2 next year' and customer demand runs 20-40% ABOVE planned capacity. 800G and 1.6T run on the SAME line and process (1.6T differs only in final test), so 800G->1.6T scaling needs minimal incremental investment.
~200k units/mo now -> >650k/mo end-2026 -> >930k/mo end-2027 (>50% from Texas); TX footprint >1.6M sqft; booked through Q2 2027

BOYD RAISED AND THE 800V PLAYBOOK: Boyd (liquid cooling — COLD PLATES + CDUs) raised to $1.8B FY2026 revenue, up from the ~$1.7B+ trajectory flagged in Q1 ($1.5B lands in Eaton's books; Boyd did $1.1B in 2025); Q2 $432M was 20% ABOVE plan; wins on being the DESIGN PARTNER embedded in chip providers' roadmaps (first look/first bid), aerospace-grade quality at scale (smaller rivals showing 'quality issues from the get-go'), and it hands Eaton an early strategic read into chip development; joins organic growth in 2027. 800V DC: content ~$3.4M PER MW CONFIRMED 'the right number'; the customer objective is TOKENS PER MEGAWATT (~5% efficiency gain from DC conversion — 'when there's so much money involved, this is going to happen'). Eaton frames FOUR technical blocks required to win 800V — (1) medium-voltage SOLID-STATE TRANSFORMER (Resilient Power, 'clearly ahead' per hyperscaler and chip-maker feedback), (2) DC BREAKER technology, (3) power electronics/power quality (UPS), (4) COOLING (Boyd) — plus a service network that arrives 'in an hour, not days'; players missing blocks 'will have a really hard time.' Prefab/modular (Fibrebond): electrician/plumber scarcity pushes modular builds, and 800V's simpler architecture INCREASES the modular opportunity, extending Eaton from gray space into white space.
Boyd raised to $1.8B FY26 (Q2 +20% vs plan); $3.4M/MW confirmed; 800V = 4 blocks (SST/DC breaker/UPS/cooling) + service; modular expands with 800V

→ Amazon: 'We continue to add content in US hyperscalers' AI deployments with DESIGN WINS SUPPORTING AWS POWER SUPPLY AND BATTERY BACKUP SYSTEMS' — creating additional content opportunities for the high-voltage portfolio including silicon carbide as architectures move toward 800V DC.

NEW AI-datacenter products: first 5 MW SOLID-STATE TRANSFORMER (indoor) prototype delivering to a hyperscaler (R&D-shared) later in 2026, 6 MW outdoor SST started with a DIFFERENT hyperscaler — SST orders '27+, gated by how fast AI factories shift to 800V DC; medium-voltage UPS 'stability block' could book orders even sooner (possibly H2 2026). H1 DC orders >$5B (2x FY25); SST 5MW to hyperscaler 2026; scope $300M/GW -> 2-3x
Hyperscalers are redesigning network architectures to address bandwidth and latency demands; transition from copper to optical connections already underway and will accelerate over the next year

Capacity conversion is the swing factor for InP epiwafer supply, and it is gated on customer commitment: "We also have the ability to flex assets and convert existing tooling to support indium phosphide growth, but this would need to be tied to concrete customer commitments." On converting GaAs lines to InP: "Our tool set is flexible to some degree. We can certainly transfer or convert capacity from our technology to the next. That kind of conversion would again need to be tied to discrete customer demand and visibility to that, because obviously it does come with downtime of the tools and also CapEx commitments." On Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy: "We are monitoring demand very closely, and as mentioned, we are converting capacities if and when that demand materializes." Additional MOCVD tools would come via LTA, customer co-funding, or tool consignment - "any kind of capacity expansion or addition of tools will need to come with customer commitments." Wafer-diameter transitions (4->6 inch, 6->8 inch) are customer-driven, with no company-wide push.
GaAs->InP tool conversion and Taiwan 6-inch InP epitaxy, both gated on concrete customer commitments (LTA / co-funding / tool consignment)

800V DC power mgmt; HV MOSFETs + polymer caps/inductors/current-sense for AI power
